**Problem.** $S_1, \dots, S_n$ are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, each a union of two closed intervals. Any three $S_i$ have a common point. Show some point belongs to $\geq n/2$ of the $S_i$.

**Strategy.** I'll prove there exist two points that together pierce (hit) every $S_i$. Then by pigeonhole, one of them lies in $\geq \lceil n/2 \rceil \geq n/2$ of the sets.

---

**Proof.**

The cases $n \leq 2$ are trivial (any point in $S_1$ lies in $\geq 1 \geq n/2$ sets). Assume $n \geq 3$.

Write each $S_i = [a_i, b_i] \cup [c_i, d_i]$ with $a_i \le b_i \le c_i \le d_i$. (If the two intervals overlap they merge into one; then $b_i = c_i$ and the "gap" $(b_i, c_i)$ is empty.) Define:

$$p = \max_{i} a_i, \qquad q = \min_{i} d_i.$$

**Step 1: $p \le q$.**

Suppose $p > q$. Choose $m$ with $a_m = p$ and $\ell$ with $d_\ell = q$. Then $a_m = p > q = d_\ell$, so every point of $S_m$ is $\ge p > q \ge$ every point of $S_\ell$, giving $S_m \cap S_\ell = \emptyset$. Pick any $k \notin \{m, \ell\}$ (exists since $n \ge 3$). Then $S_m \cap S_\ell \cap S_k = \emptyset$, contradicting the $(3,3)$-property. $\checkmark$

**Step 2: $\{p, q\}$ pierces every $S_i$.**

For every $i$: $a_i \le p$ (since $p = \max a_j$) and $q \le d_i$ (since $q = \min d_j$), and $p \le q$, so $p, q \in [a_i, d_i]$.

Suppose for contradiction that some $S_i$ contains **neither** $p$ nor $q$. Since $p, q \in [a_i, d_i]$, both must lie in the gap: $b_i < p$ and $q < c_i$, i.e., $[p,q] \subseteq (b_i, c_i)$.

Choose $m$ with $a_m = p$ and $\ell$ with $d_\ell = q$.

- **$m \ne i$ and $\ell \ne i$:** $m = i$ would give $a_i = p > b_i$, contradicting $a_i \le b_i$. Similarly $\ell = i$ gives $d_i = q < c_i \le d_i$, contradiction.

- **$S_m \cap S_\ell \cap S_i = \emptyset$:** Every point of $S_m$ is $\ge a_m = p$. Every point of $S_\ell$ is $\le d_\ell = q$. So $S_m \cap S_\ell \subseteq [p, q]$. But $S_i = [a_i, b_i] \cup [c_i, d_i]$ with $[a_i, b_i] \subseteq (-\infty, p)$ and $[c_i, d_i] \subseteq (q, +\infty)$, so $S_i \cap [p,q] = \emptyset$. Hence $S_m \cap S_\ell \cap S_i = \emptyset$.

  - **If $m \ne \ell$:** $\{m, \ell, i\}$ are three distinct indices, so the $(3,3)$-property gives $S_m \cap S_\ell \cap S_i \ne \emptyset$ — contradiction.

  - **If $m = \ell$:** Then $S_m = [p, b_m] \cup [c_m, q] \subseteq [p,q]$, so $S_m \cap S_i = \emptyset$ (as $S_i \cap [p,q] = \emptyset$). Pick any $k \notin \{m, i\}$ (exists since $n \ge 3$). The $(3,3)$-property gives $S_m \cap S_i \cap S_k \ne \emptyset$, but $S_m \cap S_i = \emptyset$ — contradiction.

In all cases we reach a contradiction, so no $S_i$ avoids both $p$ and $q$: each $S_i$ contains $p$ or $q$. $\checkmark$

**Step 3: Pigeonhole.**

Each of the $n$ sets contains $p$ or $q$. By pigeonhole, at least one of $p, q$ belongs to $\ge \lceil n/2 \rceil \ge n/2$ of the sets. $\blacksquare$

**Problem.** $S_1, \dots, S_n$ are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, each a union of two closed intervals. Any three $S_i$ have a common point. Show some point belongs to $\geq n/2$ of the $S_i$.

**Strategy.** I'll prove there exist two points that together pierce (hit) every $S_i$. Then by pigeonhole, one of them lies in $\geq \lceil n/2 \rceil \geq n/2$ of the sets.

---

**Proof.**

The cases $n \leq 2$ are trivial (any point in $S_1$ lies in $\geq 1 \geq n/2$ sets). Assume $n \geq 3$.

Write each $S_i = [a_i, b_i] \cup [c_i, d_i]$ with $a_i \le b_i \le c_i \le d_i$. (If the two intervals overlap they merge into one; then $b_i = c_i$ and the "gap" $(b_i, c_i)$ is empty.) Define:

$$p = \max_{i} a_i, \qquad q = \min_{i} d_i.$$

**Step 1: $p \le q$.**

Suppose $p > q$. Choose $m$ with $a_m = p$ and $\ell$ with $d_\ell = q$. Then $a_m = p > q = d_\ell$, so every point of $S_m$ is $\ge p > q \ge$ every point of $S_\ell$, giving $S_m \cap S_\ell = \emptyset$. Pick any $k \notin \{m, \ell\}$ (exists since $n \ge 3$). Then $S_m \cap S_\ell \cap S_k = \emptyset$, contradicting the $(3,3)$-property. $\checkmark$

**Step 2: $\{p, q\}$ pierces every $S_i$.**

For every $i$: $a_i \le p$ (since $p = \max a_j$) and $q \le d_i$ (since $q = \min d_j$), and $p \le q$, so $p, q \in [a_i, d_i]$.

Suppose for contradiction that some $S_i$ contains **neither** $p$ nor $q$. Since $p, q \in [a_i, d_i]$, both must lie in the gap: $b_i < p$ and $q < c_i$, i.e., $[p,q] \subseteq (b_i, c_i)$.

Choose $m$ with $a_m = p$ and $\ell$ with $d_\ell = q$.

- **$m \ne i$ and $\ell \ne i$:** $m = i$ would give $a_i = p > b_i$, contradicting $a_i \le b_i$. Similarly $\ell = i$ gives $d_i = q < c_i \le d_i$, contradiction.

- **$S_m \cap S_\ell \cap S_i = \emptyset$:** Every point of $S_m$ is $\ge a_m = p$. Every point of $S_\ell$ is $\le d_\ell = q$. So $S_m \cap S_\ell \subseteq [p, q]$. But $S_i = [a_i, b_i] \cup [c_i, d_i]$ with $[a_i, b_i] \subseteq (-\infty, p)$ and $[c_i, d_i] \subseteq (q, +\infty)$, so $S_i \cap [p,q] = \emptyset$. Hence $S_m \cap S_\ell \cap S_i = \emptyset$.

  - **If $m \ne \ell$:** $\{m, \ell, i\}$ are three distinct indices, so the $(3,3)$-property gives $S_m \cap S_\ell \cap S_i \ne \emptyset$ — contradiction.

**Step 3: Pigeonhole.**

Each of the $n$ sets contains $p$ or $q$. By pigeonhole, at least one of $p, q$ belongs to $\ge \lceil n/2 \rceil \ge n/2$ of the sets. $\blacksquare$
